fixed.before: Finns (Finnar) are the Sami. First stanza, in prose order: the generous prince himself found most clearly how the mighty spells of the sorcerous Finns saved the very great Thorir, when the fire-sender of the mast-heads struck the Hound across the shoulders with the gold-adorned sword; smooth, it would hardly bite. 'Fire-sender of the mast-heads' is evidently a kenning for Olaf as a generous lord; its exact construal is uncertain. Second stanza, roughly: the fir of gold [a man] who taunts Thorir denies true valour; I know this from home: who would see greater deeds than the great-hearted Hound's, when the might of the storm of cross-fences [battle; its might, a warrior, i.e. Thorir], he who pressed forward, dared to strike against the king-man of Gunnrann? 'Cross-fences' are probably shields; 'Gunnrann' ('battle-hall') is obscure, the phrase evidently meaning King Olaf. The manuscript's 'kononɢ manni' is taken as one word. The construal of this half-stanza is uncertain.
fixed.after: Finns (Finnar) are the Sami. First stanza, in prose order: the generous prince himself found most clearly how the mighty spells of the sorcerous Finns saved the very great Thorir, when the fire-sender of the mast-heads struck the Hound across the shoulders with the gold-adorned sword; smooth, it would hardly bite. 'Fire-sender of the mast-heads' is evidently a kenning for Olaf as a generous lord; its exact construal is uncertain. Second stanza, roughly: the fir of gold [a man] who taunts Thorir denies true valour; I know this from home: who would see greater deeds than the great-hearted Hound's, when the might of the storm of cross-fences [battle; its might, a warrior, i.e. Thorir], he who pressed forward, dared to strike against the king's man? 'Cross-fences' are probably shields, and 'battle-hall' (Gunnrann) is a shield too, part of the same kenning; 'kononɢ manni' is 'the king's man', King Olaf. The construal of this half-stanza is uncertain.

fixed.before: The transcription lacks some letters: 'arka', 'erkr' and 'oꝛkum' are read as forms of mǫrk, 'mark'; 'bte' as bǿte, 'let [her] pay'; 'liis' as langlífis; 'ꝼtr' as fǿtr, 'feet'; 'haa' as hafa, 'have'. 'He' in 7v.11 is not named here, probably the bishop. Finns are the Sami, visited for soothsaying. 'Heathen' in 7v.18 means unbaptised; the practice is not explained. 'hor' (7v.23) is read as 'hair', uncertainly; 'frauða fǿtr' as frogs' feet. 'til jafns réttar' (7v.1a-2a) is translated literally; its legal sense is unclear. 'dyð' (7v.8b) is uncertain. bókmál (7v.19a), 'book-speech', is taken as the written church law.

fixed.before: 1.43–44 end a stanza begun in the context: the bold receiver of the 'steed of the fair wind' (a ship), i.e. the ruler, draws under himself with true words the pine-haired waiting-wife of Thridi (Odin), that is Earth: he wins the land. biꝼkvan is read as biðkván, 'waiting-wife'. Hroptatyr and Ygg are names of Odin. 1.51–54 are obscure: the land-holder (the ruler) seems to reward with a headband the 'shaper of the gods' fjord' (poetry), i.e. the poet; hunn, taken as 'mast-head', is unexplained. 1.55–58 are also obscure: the cargo of Gunnlod's arms and the waterfall of horns are both the mead of poetry; hlitstyggr, 'averse to enough', seems to describe a generous lord.

fixed.before: The 'gnawer of carrion' is the giant Thiazi in eagle form; he is also 'Hymir's kin-tree'. The wolf's father, Thor's confidant, Lopt, the mover of hosts and the girdle-thief of the gods' Brising are Loki. The maid who knew the Aesir's cure for old age, the lady of Brunnakr's brook, is Idunn. The stone-Nidad is a giant, so his courts are the giants' world. sorg-æyra (1.557) is uncertain, and may describe Loki or the maid.

not_upheld.n5#1: The translator read seiðstaðr ('sorcery place') as seiðstafr ('sorcery staff'), an object found with the bones, and says so in the note: a marked, defensible emendation, not an error.
not_upheld.n4#8: róta is the genitive plural of rót: 'the roots of the ear-tree of the raging beast' is the horn, the standard construal, explained in the note; the infinitive reading leaves 'vil ek orð' without sense.
